title: Research Bite #45: Deployment of Teaching Assistants Guidance Report
author: Craig Barton
summary: Research Bite #45 summarizes the Education Endowment Foundation's updated Deployment of Teaching Assistants guidance report, which synthesizes dozens of studies plus expert consultation into recommendations for how schools should use teaching assistants (TAs) in mainstream classrooms. Its central principle is that TAs should supplement, not replace, the classroom teacher — pupils who struggle most should spend at least as much time with the teacher as everyone else, if not more, meaning TA support is not a substitute for teacher attention to the lowest-attaining and SEND pupils. The report's five recommendations cover ensuring TAs facilitate access to high-quality teaching, using scaffolding to build pupil independence rather than dependency, delivering structured evidence-based interventions with clear objectives, preparing and training staff properly, and getting whole-school buy-in for implementation. A recurring caution running through the guidance is that poorly managed TA deployment can backfire — pupils becoming over-reliant on TA support is named as a real risk. Because effective deployment depends on whole-school strategic decisions rather than something a single teacher can fix alone, Barton frames this primarily as a guidance report for school leaders that individual teachers still need to actively engage with.
points: The central principle is unambiguous: TAs should supplement, not replace, the teacher — pupils who struggle most should get at least as much teacher time as everyone else, not less.
Teachers retain primary responsibility for the learning of all pupils, especially low-prior-attaining pupils and pupils with SEND, even when a TA is present.
A named risk of poorly managed TA support is pupils becoming over-dependent on it or spending too much time away from core classroom teaching, which can hinder rather than help independence.
Effective TA deployment is a whole-school leadership problem (training, role clarity, communication systems), not something an individual teacher can fix in isolation.
quotes: This guidance report from the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) offers comprehensive recommendations for optimising the deployment of teaching assistants (TAs) in mainstream schools.

It emphasises that TAs should supplement, rather than replace, direct teacher instruction, particularly for students needing extra support, including those with special educational needs and disabilities (SEND).
Teachers retain primary responsibility for the learning of all pupils, especially low-prior-attaining pupils and pupils with SEND.
there's a risk TAs might unintentionally hinder pupil independence or replace teacher instruction, leading to negative outcomes or over-reliance.
TAs should supplement – not replace – the teacher. This means that pupils who struggle most should spend at least as much time with the teacher as other pupils, if not more.

The document outlines five key recommendations: ensuring TAs facilitate access to high-quality teaching, promoting student independence through scaffolding, effectively delivering evidence-based interventions, preparing and training staff for TA deployment, and engaging all staff in the implementation process.
